opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the more important and somewhat underappreciated questions. The basic picture is: if you look at a lot of the empirical results, performance tends to scale roughly log-linearly with inference compute. Each doubling of the tokens or samples you throw at a problem buys you some roughly constant increment of performance, at least over some range. That's diminishing returns in an absolute sense, since each additional unit of compute gets you less, but it's not the kind of diminishing returns where you hit a wall and it flattens out completely.

The key question is how long that log-linear regime holds and what it looks like at the frontier. A few things I think about.

First, there's a distinction between methods that are "dumb" in how they use compute, like best-of-n sampling or majority voting, and methods where the model is actually reasoning for longer in a coherent way. Best-of-n saturates pretty quickly. If the model basically never generates the right answer, sampling a million times doesn't help, and if you don't have a good verifier, you can't pick out the right answer anyway. Whereas with long chains of reasoning that are trained with RL, the model can, in principle, do something more like what a human does when they work on a problem for a week. It can try approaches, notice they fail, backtrack, and build up intermediate results. That kind of inference scaling seems much less likely to saturate early, because it's more like extending the serial depth of thought.

Second, it really depends on the task. For tasks with easy verification, like math with a checkable answer or code with tests, you can get a lot out of extra inference compute, because search plus verification is powerful. For fuzzier tasks, like research taste, strategy, or writing, it's less clear, and I'd expect returns to drop off faster unless the model is also good at evaluating its own work.

Third, there's an important interaction with model capability. A weaker model given 100x the inference compute often doesn't match a stronger model with 1x. There's some exchange rate between training compute and inference compute, but it's not unlimited. Past a certain point, you're bottlenecked on the model's underlying competence, its ability to notice its own mistakes, and things like that. So I tend to think of inference compute as something that can buy you maybe the equivalent of a meaningful but bounded jump in effective capability, rather than an arbitrary amount.

Where this matters most for me is in thinking about the dynamics around AI automating AI R&D. If you have a model that's around the level of a decent research engineer, the question is whether you can run lots of copies, have them think for a long time, and get a big speedup. My overall guess is that inference scaling will be a big deal there, especially for parallel throughput, since you can just run many more instances. But I'd be somewhat skeptical of claims that you can take a mediocre model and just throw enormous inference at it to get superhuman performance on open-ended tasks. The returns curve probably bends down more on those tasks.

So, to summarize, I'd say we have real but diminishing returns, roughly logarithmic, with the most important uncertainties being how well models can use very long serial reasoning and how much verification bottlenecks things outside of easily checkable domains.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that there are pretty clearly diminishing returns, but the question is how fast they set in and whether you can keep finding new ways to spend the compute.

The way I think about it is that there are a few different ways you can use inference compute, and they have different scaling properties. The simplest one is just: run the model longer on the problem. Chain of thought, let it think for 10,000 tokens instead of 1,000. And that seems to give you pretty substantial gains up to a point, but it's a log-linear kind of relationship at best. You spend 10x more and you get some fixed increment of capability, and then another 10x gets you a similar increment, and eventually the model just runs out of useful things to do with the extra thinking. It starts going in circles or it's already found the answer and can't verify it any better.

Then there's the sampling and selection approach, where you generate a bunch of attempts and pick the best one. If you have a good verifier, like a unit test or a proof checker, this can scale surprisingly well, because you're basically just buying lottery tickets and the verifier tells you when you've won. But if you don't have a good verifier, which is the case for most real tasks, you're relying on the model to judge its own outputs, and then the returns taper off pretty quickly. You see this in the pass@k curves: the gap between pass@1 and pass@100 can be huge on coding benchmarks, but the gap between what you actually get out with a learned reranker and pass@1 is a lot smaller.

And then there's the agentic stuff, where the model is running in a loop, taking actions, getting feedback from the environment, and this is the one I think is most interesting for the diminishing returns question. Because there, extra compute isn't just thinking harder, it's also gathering more information. You run more experiments, you read more of the codebase, you try more approaches. And in principle that doesn't have the same ceiling, because the environment keeps giving you new signal. But in practice current models seem to hit a wall where they stop making progress, they get confused, they lose track of what they were doing. So the effective horizon is bounded by something like the model's ability to maintain coherence over a long trajectory, not by the compute budget per se.

The thing I'd really emphasize though is that this isn't static. A big part of what training does is make the model better at using inference compute. So the returns curve you measure today is a property of today's models, and the next generation is going to have a different curve, probably one where the useful range extends further. The reasoning models were a pretty dramatic example of this: you took basically the same base model and trained it to actually benefit from thinking longer, and suddenly the inference scaling curve looked totally different.

So if someone asks me "do we hit diminishing returns?", I'd say yes, obviously, at any fixed level of training. But the more decision-relevant question is whether labs can keep pushing that frontier out, and I think the answer there is probably yes for a while. The place I'd be most uncertain is the very long horizon stuff, like can you get something useful out of a model running for a week on a problem. My guess is that for current models, no, not really, most of that compute is wasted. But that's exactly the capability that would matter most for things like automating AI research, so it's the one I'd watch most closely.

astra-6.text:
I think you should expect diminishing returns, but the important question is how quickly they set in, and how that compares to the difficulty of the tasks you care about.

For example, you could give a model more compute by having it generate a bunch of candidate answers and then pick the best one. That can work pretty well if you have a reliable way to check the answers. But if the model keeps making the same mistake, or if it can’t distinguish a good answer from a plausible but wrong answer, then sampling more won’t necessarily help very much.

There’s also a distinction between giving today’s models more time to think and training models to use that extra time effectively. You might see a particular model plateau, but that doesn’t establish that inference compute in general has hit a limit. It might mean you need a different training procedure to make productive use of longer reasoning.

So I’d be somewhat sceptical of extrapolating either way. I wouldn’t assume that you can turn an arbitrarily weak model into an arbitrarily strong one just by running it for longer. But I also wouldn’t take diminishing returns as much reassurance. You could have quite substantial diminishing returns and still get an economically important improvement from spending ten or a hundred times more compute on a sufficiently valuable task.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you should expect diminishing returns, but the important question is how quickly they set in, and whether better methods keep pushing that point out.

For example, suppose you give a model more time by having it generate a hundred candidate answers. That can help a lot if you have a reliable way to identify which answer is correct. But if the model makes the same mistake across all those attempts, or your process for choosing an answer is itself unreliable, then you might get relatively little benefit.

So I’d distinguish between problems where checking an answer is much easier than finding it, and problems where evaluation is almost as hard as doing the task. In the first case, there’s a fairly straightforward route to getting value from more inference compute. In the second case, you need something more sophisticated, and it’s less clear how far that scales.

There’s also a distinction between giving a fixed model more compute and training models to use additional compute effectively. Seeing a particular prompting strategy plateau wouldn’t establish that inference compute in general has hit a limit.

My overall view is that diminishing returns are quite plausible, but that alone doesn’t tell us whether the gains will be small. You can have diminishing returns and still get very substantial improvements over the range of compute that matters economically.
